newsitem.title: TANZANIA: More Rwandan Hutu refugees flee camps in Tanzania.
newsitem.headline: More Rwandan Hutu refugees flee camps in Tanzania.

text.p: Some 35,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees abandoned camps in northwestern Tanzania overnight and others continue to join the mass exodus to avoid repatriation to Rwanda, U.N. refugee agency officials said on Thursday.
The officials said 600 Burundians, fleeing an increasingly ferocious guerrilla war in their country, have also decamped.
The flight by the refugees came a day after U.N. officials said between 10,000 and 13,000 Rwandan Moslem refugees had agreed to go back home in voluntary repatriation.
The Moslems are outside the Hutu-Tutsi divide in Rwandan society and few played any part in the massacres in Rwanda in 1994, when militant Hutus killed up to one million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
Heavily armed Tanzanian army troops moved into the area around the camps on Thursday but it was unclear whether they would try to force the refugees back to their camps.
UNHCR officials told Reuters that the refugees fled camps at Kitale, Lukole and Keza and were heading southeast in hopes of reaching Zambia and Malawi.

"They (refugees) do not want to return to Rwanda at all. We have offered them assistance to return to their camps but they have rejected this. Countries they want to go to are Kenya, Uganda, Zambia and Malawi," said Anette Nyekan, head of the UNHCR mission at Karagwe.
Another aid worker said security had broken down in camps abandoned by the fleeing refugees, most of whom were hostile towards the United Nations.
On Tuesday some 15,000 refugees fled camps in the northwest after Tanzania and the UNHCR last week gave all refugees until December 31 to return to Rwanda.

Officials blame the refugee flight on intimidation of the refugees by the Interahamwe, Rwandan Hutu militiamen who led the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. The Interahamwe are determined not to return home because they fear reprisals or prosecution.
"In eastern Zaire and over here, one of the problems we face is there has always been a certain number of intimidators in the camps," an aid official said.
"We do know every time someone wants to go home there is pressure put on them to change their mind and that is still going on," said Anne Willem Bijleveld, a UNHCR official.
Nyekan said refugees were continuing to flee camps dotted around the northwestern region and figures were sure to rise sharply later in the day.
The Tanzanian army deployed heavily armed troops in Ngara after the refugees fled and the local radio warned the refugees they faced deportation or arrest for abandoning the camps.
It was unclear whether Tanzania, traditionally hospitable towards refugees, would use its troops. The army has some 10,000 men in the region but it has not yet tried to round up refugees.
"The Tanzanians have to do something now, what choice do they have now, except to send in the army? It is a nightmare," said a senior aid official in Ngara.

Nyekan said a Tanzanian delegation sent to the camps to explain why the 542,000 Rwandan refugees must return to their tiny, ethnically divided central African country by the end of the month failed to achieve any positive results.

The Tanzania-UNHCR repatriation plan has been attacked by the London-based human rights group Amnesty International and the exiled Hutu lobby group Rally for the Return of Refugees and Democracy in Rwanda.
The two institutions accuse UNHCR of abandoning its principle of protecting refugees against forced repatriation. Tanzania has not said what will happen to those who refuse to return voluntarily.
